items.source: Dark Side of the Boom — FOMC Take
items.title: The 'every-other-meeting Fed': pause in Oct, hike in Dec to 4–4.25%, March in the tail
items.idea: No hike in October, but the statement upgraded activity from 'solid' to 'strong' and added 'accumulation of more information' language. Base case is a final December hike to 4.00–4.25%; March stays alive if inflation runs hot. Warsh said policy is 'working' and financial conditions are tighter but not restrictive.
items.angle: Pause-hike-pause is a cadence, not a pivot. Curve steepened, so duration still pays the price for 'patience'.
items.tweetA: A Fed that says 'strong' growth and 'patience' in the same statement isn't pausing, it's scheduling. December is the trade; October was the setup. The 10y near 5% already knows.
items.tweetB: Everyone is debating whether the Fed is done. Wrong question. The question is whether a hike every second meeting is tightening or just slower tightening. The long end is voting for 'slower, therefore longer'.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom — FOMC Take
items.title: Warsh removes live meetings from the calendar: strategy-only FOMCs from fall 2027
items.idea: The FOMC keeps eight meetings a year, but one in 2027 and two in 2028 become strategy meetings with no statement and no vote. Task-force reports are due by year-end with framework changes considered in Q1 2027. The author reads it as removing dates from the roulette wheel.
items.angle: Fewer live dates compress event vol into the remaining ones. Worth thinking about what that does to FOMC-day gamma pricing.
items.tweetA: Warsh just deleted three FOMC decision dates from 2027-28. Fewer scheduled catalysts means each remaining one carries more weight. Vol sellers should read the calendar before the statement.
items.tweetB: The Fed is rewriting its own framework in public while hiking. Strategy meetings with no vote, a task force due in Q1 2027. Watch which direction the new framework leans.

items.title: Fed hold with 2 dissents; MacroEdge still calls peak yields and re-levers long bonds on selloffs
items.idea: Statement upgraded growth to 'strong'; the Fed cuts meetings from 8 to 7 in 2027 and 6 in 2028. The author still thinks peak yields are in and will use any long-bond selloff to re-lever. The book is +11.1% vs -0.4% for SPX since the Oct 6 launch, pulled back 1.63% on the Fed selloff, and is long rates and rate-sensitives.
items.angle: Direct opposite positioning to Capital Flows' policy-error view. Two public, opposed reads on the same meeting.
items.tweetA: Same FOMC, two opposite trades. One shop is re-levering long bonds on every selloff, another says the Fed is ignoring inflation. The 10y near 5% is where one of them gets carried out.
items.tweetB: +11.1% vs -0.4% for SPX in 17 sessions, built on long duration into a hiking Fed. Either it's the best-timed peak-yield call of the cycle or a short-vol trade with a rates fuse. Month-end tells.

items.title: Capex reflex flips: ORCL guides peak capex and rises, MSFT guides FCF-positive 2027 and rises, GOOG guides 'significantly higher' 2027 and plunges
items.idea: Three hyperscaler prints, three different market answers to the same capex question. The market now pays for capex discipline and punishes open-ended spend. The author's thesis: the data-center construction cycle peaks this quarter or next, possibly Q1.
items.angle: Stock reaction function to capex has inverted since 2024. Picks-and-shovels suppliers carry the order-book risk if the buyers are rewarded for spending less.
items.tweetA: ORCL: peak capex, stock up. MSFT: FCF positive in 2027, stock up. GOOG: capex up again, stock -10%. The market just repriced the AI trade from 'who spends most' to 'who stops first'. Suppliers should be nervous.
items.tweetB: For two years capex guides were the bullish catalyst for $NVDA $AVGO $VRT. If the buyers get rewarded for spending less, the supplier revenue line is the thing being cut. Nobody on the Alphabet call said that out loud.

items.title: Data-center build peak thesis: politicians change seats, environmental lawsuits get teeth around the turn of the year
items.idea: Beyond capex guides, the author argues a political and legal lag will bite: seat changes after the midterms and environmental groups spooling up litigation, with Q1 possible for the peak. This is a non-financial brake on the buildout.
items.angle: Permitting and litigation risk is a supply-side constraint on AI infra not priced in earnings models. Watch local moratoria.
items.tweetA: Everyone models AI capex off hyperscaler guidance. Nobody models the zoning board. Midterms plus a lawsuit pipeline is how a data-center boom actually slows down.
items.tweetB: The AI buildout's binding constraint keeps changing: chips, then power, now maybe permits and lawyers. Each one hits a different part of the supply chain. Which of those do you own?

items.title: Breadth reset: only 41% of stocks above the 50D while S&P sits 120bps from ATH, Fear & Greed still in 'Fear'
items.idea: QQQ is +300bps on the week, Dow +60bps; rebound in momentum/growth and out of value/low-vol. % above 20D is back to 55% (neutral), % above 50D at 41% (still slightly oversold). The Anthropic S-1 was 'much better than feared'. Fear & Greed has only just left 'Extreme Fear'.
items.angle: Index at highs, sentiment in fear, breadth damaged: a classic setup where the index lies about the average stock.
items.tweetA: S&P is 120bps from highs and Fear & Greed says 'Fear'. Only 41% of stocks are above their 50D. Index-level calm is hiding a very different market underneath.
items.tweetB: Eliant credits Anthropic's S-1 coming in 'better than feared' as part of the QQQ +300bps week. A private lab's filing is now an input to index sentiment. That's a new kind of macro event.

items.title: The end of non-OPEC supply growth: US shale plateau at 13–14 mb/d, associated gas diverging from crude
items.idea: HFIR's real-time tracker shows no US growth despite two quarters of favorable prices; producers only added associated gas. Shale, Canada and Brazil have peaked; Argentina, Guyana and Colombia can add ~0.4 mb/d but decline offsets it. Venezuela gains are offset by Russian declines.
items.angle: With WTI near $100, zero shale response is the signal. The supply elasticity everyone assumes isn't there.
items.tweetA: WTI at $100 for two quarters and US shale produced more gas, not more oil. The price cure for high prices has stopped working. That's not a cycle, that's a ceiling.
items.tweetB: Argentina + Guyana + Colombia add ~0.4 mb/d. The 'drill baby drill' balance requires 10x that. Do that math before pricing any Iran deal into crude.

charts.desc: Real-time US crude production tracker flat at 13–14 mb/d; associated gas vs crude divergence 🔥 CHART WORTH SAVING

items.title: Hormuz outcome decides the oil balance: 3–4 mb/d deficit, 4–5 mb/d Middle East shut-in
items.idea: Market deficit is 3–4 mb/d with 8 mb/d flowing via the Oman lane. Shut-ins: ~2.5 mb/d Saudi, ~1.8 mb/d Iran. 'Iran wins = tight, US wins = loose.' With non-OPEC growth gone, there are no short-term valves.
items.angle: Binary on one strait with no supply buffer behind it. Asymmetric if talks fail.
items.tweetA: Iran wins, oil stays tight. US wins, oil loosens. Either way there's no non-OPEC valve behind it. That's the cleanest binary in commodities and the options market is treating it as a coin flip.
items.tweetB: Shut-in Saudi 2.5 mb/d plus Iran 1.8 mb/d. Add the 8 mb/d rerouted through Oman. One pipeline problem away from a worse number. $XOM $OXY $MPC

items.title: 'Running in the Sand': WTI $98–108 is the most important range of the cycle and will be 'violently defended'
items.idea: After an October move higher, the author expects a pre-midterm fire hose of headlines and active intervention (Bessent, Lutnick, Trump) around the range. SPR is at record lows and there's no aggregate demand destruction. Above 108 opens new pathways. Rage directed at Iran possible post-election.
items.angle: Treat the range as a policy-capped band, so breakout is a policy-failure signal.
items.tweetA: WTI $98–108 is being defended by people with SPR and a podium. Range-bound until intervention fails. When it fails, it fails fast. SPR at record lows is the loaded gun, not the shield.
items.tweetB: Headline whipsaw until the midterms: a 3:59pm ET Vance-Iran story, then a denial. Trading that tape is a tax. The edge is waiting for the range break, not predicting it.

charts.desc: WTI chart zoomed into the 98–108 range with 3:59pm ET headline spike

items.title: Capital cycle toward 'real things' and 'phony wealth' mean reversion
items.idea: The author argues we're in early innings of a rotation from asset-owner 'Powell's Valhalla' toward the old-world economy. Concentrated, borrowed wealth tends to mean-revert, possibly through acute scarcity rather than a clean reset. Roadmap update due Friday.
items.angle: Thematic frame: old-world capex (energy, grid, materials) vs financial-asset wealth. Pairs with the copper and non-OPEC pieces.
items.tweetA: Two years of 'asset owners do nothing and win'. The next phase may be 'owners of real things do nothing and win'. Same lazy trade, different assets.
items.tweetB: Phony wealth is wealth you can't eat, burn or build with. The test for the next cycle is which balance sheets hold molecules.

items.title: 'The Fed's Looming Policy Error': pausing with zero forward guidance into rising inflation
items.idea: Thesis: by pausing and not guiding more hikes, the Fed let the forward curve price fewer hikes while inflation rises, which does the opposite of the stated goal. 'Actions are louder than words.' The author argues Warsh gave no clear reason for the pause, and that positioning underestimates it.
items.angle: Direct challenge to the 'patient Fed' consensus. Cross-check with Authers on 2y yields easing during the presser.
items.tweetA: If the Fed won't guide hikes, the market guides them lower. Two-year yields fell during the press conference. That is the opposite of what a central bank trying to tighten wants.
items.tweetB: The consensus: Fed pauses, patient. The contrarian read: Fed pauses while saying 'strong' growth, curve prices fewer hikes. Both can't hold. Watch breakevens for the verdict.

items.source: Bloomberg — John Authers, Points of Return
items.title: Warsh's 3 min 16 sec non-answer to 'why not hike today?'
items.idea: Two FOMC members dissented in favor of a hike, including Lisa Cook. Warsh didn't answer the October question, refused follow-ups, and said 'the goal isn't to throw sand in the gears.' Market expects a 4.6% peak within 12 months; market-based inflation expectations rose, which Authers attributes to the Fed rather than the administration this time.
items.angle: Breakevens rising on a Fed event is a credibility signal. Fed dissent to the hawkish side with a governor under political pressure is notable.
items.tweetA: Two dissents for a hike, one of them Lisa Cook. Warsh took 3 minutes 16 seconds to not answer 'why not hike now'. Breakevens rose. The last two inflation-expectation spikes were Trump's fault. This one's the Fed's.
items.tweetB: Fed funds peak priced at 4.6%. The dissent says the committee is split on timing, not direction. Watch the December minutes language, not the presser.

items.source: Bloomberg — John Authers, Points of Return
items.title: 'Peak Capex': MSFT capex $45.2B vs $45.9B est., Alphabet's 'how do we pay for it' problem
items.idea: Azure +48% to $33.2B, revenue +19% to $92.3B on capex slightly under estimate. Alphabet ad revenue $82B vs $83.6B est.; EPS $2.12 vs $3.02 (with an $8.66B paper loss on stakes like SpaceX); second straight quarter of negative FCF. Meta is seeking up to $95B in equity. Shareholders are now helping fund the buildout.
items.angle: The market sorted hyperscalers by funding model, not demand. Equity-funded capex is the new tell.
items.tweetA: Alphabet's shareholders are now funding the AI buildout. Two straight quarters of negative FCF plus Meta's $95B equity raise. When the AI bill goes to the equity market, 'peak capex' stops being a view and becomes a constraint.
items.tweetB: Microsoft: Azure +48%, capex under estimate, stock up. Alphabet: Cloud strong, FCF negative, stock -10%. The market isn't judging demand. It's judging who needs outside money.

items.source: Bloomberg — John Authers, Points of Return
items.title: Bank of Canada hikes hours before the Fed holds
items.idea: The BoC hiked on the same day the Fed paused, per the lead bullets in Authers. His line: 'Why not just get on with the job?' given the BoC had 'bitten the bullet' a few hours earlier.
items.angle: Relative-policy gap now favors CAD on carry if the Fed keeps waiting.
items.tweetA: BoC hiked. Fed paused. Same day, same inflation problem, different reaction function. If the Fed sits out until December, $USDCAD has an opinion.
items.tweetB: Central banks are splitting on timing, not direction. That divergence is where the FX trades come from, not the headline rate level.

items.source: Bloomberg — John Authers, Points of Return
items.title: UK's Healey unveils a 10% tax rate for entrepreneurs
items.idea: A new 10% tax rate for entrepreneurs with startups was announced by the UK chancellor, listed in the day's points with the Bloomberg link. Details are in the linked article, not the newsletter body.
items.angle: Tax-competition signal for founder location. Worth opening the article for the thresholds.
items.tweetA: UK just put a 10% rate on entrepreneurs. Every founder weighing Delaware vs London now has a spreadsheet to update.
items.tweetB: Tax policy is the cheapest industrial policy. A 10% rate costs little in revenue and could pull in the one input money can't buy: founders.

items.title: Google TPU becomes merchant silicon: OpenAI to buy, Oracle to rent, Anthropic ~$400B committed
items.idea: OpenAI plans to buy TPUs, with a job listing for an engineer to optimize frontier models on them. Oracle will offer TPU 8t (training) and 8i (inference) on OCI from 2027, the first non-Google major cloud to do so. Anthropic's S-1 ties ~$400B of its ~$800B compute commitments to TPUs: $161.2B Broadcom leases, $114.5B Google Cloud, plus $125–150B estimated 2028–31.
items.angle: Nvidia's largest customer going multi-chip (Broadcom, AMD, Amazon, Cerebras, TPU) is the real structural story.
items.tweetA: OpenAI committed ~$600B to Nvidia through 2030, and also lined up Broadcom, AMD, Cerebras, Trainium, now TPUs. The biggest customer is hedging the supplier. $NVDA's moat is CUDA, and OpenAI may open-source the tool that weakens it.
items.tweetB: Half of Anthropic's ~$800B compute commitments sit on Google silicon. A lab built mostly on TPUs is the proof point. $GOOGL $AVGO had the quiet quarter; the market sold the stock anyway.

items.title: TD Cowen: TPUs a $9.4B H2 business becoming $138B by 2028, ~34% of Google Cloud
items.idea: Google Cloud Q3 revenue +103% to $30.7B, operating income $11.1B vs $3.6B a year ago (~36% margin). TD Cowen sees $138B TPU revenue in 2028 versus Nvidia consensus of ~$692B in FY ending Jan 2028, roughly a fifth. Last November the Meta pitch talked of 10% of Nvidia's revenue; estimates doubled.
items.angle: If TPU revenue becomes 34% of Cloud, Google's valuation framework shifts from ads/search to silicon vendor.
items.tweetA: Cloud op income $3.6B to $11.1B in a year. TD Cowen puts TPUs at $138B by 2028. At 20% of Nvidia's size it's not a rounding error. The stock fell 10% on the same day. Choose which number you believe.
items.tweetB: Wall Street is valuing Google's AI chips as a standalone business, while selling the stock over the capex to build them. A sum-of-the-parts argument and an FCF argument in one print.

items.title: Alphabet capex: $51.4B in a quarter, 2026 at $195–205B, 'significantly' more in 2027
items.idea: Quarterly capex more than doubled YoY; full-year guide held; 2027 higher. The stock fell more than 10% after hours on capex and negative FCF. Nvidia simultaneously invests $3B in Meta's stock offering as Meta expands Nvidia use for agents.
items.angle: Supplier financing circle: Nvidia investing in customers' equity raises. Look at who funds whom.
items.tweetA: Nvidia is investing $3B in Meta's share offering so Meta can buy Nvidia chips. Vendor financing has a long history. It is rarely the good part of the chapter.
items.tweetB: $51.4B a quarter is $205B a year. The guide holds, 2027 goes 'significantly' higher, and the market's response was to take 10% off the market cap. Even Alphabet's own cash flow can't underwrite this alone.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom — Nomura McElligott note
items.title: 'Cleansing': AI complex stabilises but hedge funds are hypersensitive to the Mag 7, mutual funds near record-low exposure
items.idea: McElligott sees stabilisation after two weeks of deleveraging, options vol retreating, with Anthropic economics, capital absorption and semi earnings helping. The imbalance: HFs very sensitive to the Mag 7, mutual funds historically underweight, which could amplify an upside chase.
items.angle: Underweight real money plus long-biased HFs is an upside-chase setup, but Alphabet just showed the downside gap.
items.tweetA: Mutual funds are near record-low Mag 7 exposure while hedge funds are all-in. Every disappointment gaps down (see $GOOGL -10%), every beat gets a chase from the underweights. That's the definition of unstable.
items.tweetB: October's HF stop-outs weren't a model failure, per Nomura, they were excess leverage getting cleaned. That's the bullish read. The bearish read: leverage is repaired slower than confidence.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom — Nomura McElligott note
items.title: Momentum and carry strategies still suffering from crowding even as AI stabilises
items.idea: Beneath the AI recovery, momentum and carry strategies are still hurt by crowded positioning; the author cites hedge fund stop-outs in a month where diversification 'was temporarily suspended'.
items.angle: Crowded momentum/carry unwinds explain index-vs-breadth divergence (cf. Eliant's 41% above 50D).
items.tweetA: Momentum and carry are both still bleeding while QQQ rips. The rally is narrower than the index says, and the pain is in the strategies that were supposed to be diversifiers.
items.tweetB: A month where momentum, carry and AI all fell together is a covariance event, not a stock-picking one. Correlation is the risk factor nobody sized.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom (Bloomberg's Frank Monkam)
items.title: Dr. Copper's new dilemma: 0.25 correlation to ISM, R² of 0.06
items.idea: Copper's correlation with the ISM manufacturing PMI is just 0.25 (R² 0.06), while its correlation with tech equities heads toward 3-year highs on data centres, electrification and semis. Rising real yields and tighter credit threaten AI capex and copper could reprice financially before physical demand moves. China is ~56% of refined demand; implied vol near 1-year lows.
items.angle: Copper is now a levered AI-financing proxy. Cheap vol on a metal with a new macro driver.
items.tweetA: Copper's R² to ISM is 0.06. Its beta to tech equities is at 3-year highs. The 'global growth barometer' is now an AI-credit barometer. $FCX $COPX
items.tweetB: Copper implied vol at 1-year lows while its macro driver has just changed from Chinese property to AI bond issuance. Cheap optionality, expensive complacency.

items.title: 'Fasten Your Seatbelts': several analysts expect a flash risk-off; Bitcoin won't be unaffected
items.idea: Monthly Pro report covers macro headwinds, BTC relative performance, market internal structure, momentum indicators and a Strive vs Metaplanet comparison of mid-tier treasury companies. The intro notes a 'chorus of concerns' about an incoming flash risk-off event.
items.angle: BTC treasury companies (Strive, Metaplanet) are the levered beta; the mNAV compression risk shows up first there.
items.tweetA: When the on-chain purist writes 'fasten your seatbelts', look at the treasury companies first. They are the levered expression of BTC in a risk-off.
items.tweetB: The better question than 'will BTC drop in a crash' is 'what comes next': James Check says look through it. Treasury companies are the stress test.

items.title: Meta's 'Muse' rule of three: agent, ad-creative model, and the base model under both
items.idea: Meta's Muse brand spans products and models (Muse Code, Muse API, Muse Wonder). The post focuses on three that matter to small-business advertisers: an agent, a model that changes ad creatives, and the underlying model, with a cheat-sheet graphic.
items.angle: AI-generated ad creative is the monetisation path for Meta's capex; ties to its $95B equity raise.
items.tweetA: Meta is spending to raise up to $95B so Muse can write the ad. The capex-to-ad-revenue chain is now one product name long.
items.tweetB: Small-business advertisers are the marginal buyer of AI-generated creative. If Muse lifts conversion, Meta funds its buildout. If not, the equity raise was the first of many.
